scenes.title: A Glitch in the OS
scenes.narration_text:
Stone Age emotions. Medieval institutions. Godlike technology.

This is not a bug. It's the operating system.
scenes.context: Introductory statement contrasting human biology, societal structures, and modern technology.

scenes.title: Lethal Side Effects
scenes.narration_text: And the operating system is trying to kill you with nuclear weapons and preventable disease simultaneously.
scenes.context: The narrator explains the existential risks posed by our outdated biological 'software'.

scenes.title: The Selfish Gene
scenes.narration_text:
The Selfish Gene Made You Illogical (It Was a Good Idea at the Time).

Richard Dawkins put it perfectly:
scenes.context: Introduction of evolutionary biology concepts and the influential work of Richard Dawkins.

scenes.title: Genetic Vehicles
scenes.narration_text: "We are survival machines, robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes.".
scenes.context: A direct quote from Dawkins explaining humans as biological vessels for genetic survival.

scenes.title: Chemical Puppetry
scenes.narration_text: Translation: You're a meat puppet controlled by chemicals whose entire business plan is "make more chemicals before something eats us.".
scenes.context: A blunt simplification of human motivation as driven by primal survival instincts.

scenes.title: Gene Motive
scenes.narration_text: Your genes don't care if you're happy. They don't care if you live past thirty. They care about exactly one thing:
scenes.context: Describing the indifference of evolution toward individual well-being or longevity.

scenes.title: Ancient Engineering
scenes.narration_text:
making copies of themselves before something with teeth finds you.

For ninety-nine point nine percent of human history, this was brilliant engineering.
scenes.context: Explaining how genetic survival was the primary goal for the vast majority of human existence.

scenes.title: Outdated Instincts
scenes.narration_text: Now it's why you distrust strangers you need to cooperate with, build weapons you'll never use, and fight over territory you don't need.
scenes.context: Contrasting ancient survival traits with their detrimental effects in the modern world.

scenes.title: Biological Mismatch
scenes.narration_text:
The genes are still celebrating. You are not.

Part 1: Your Brain Was Optimized for a World That Doesn't Exist.
scenes.context: The transition into the first section of the book regarding the brain's mismatch with modern life.

scenes.title: The Violence Module
scenes.narration_text:
The Violence Module (Or: Why You Tend to Prefer Bombs Over Band-Aids).

Fifteen to thirty percent of your ancestors died from violence.
scenes.context: Introduction of the 'Violence Module' and historical statistics on human mortality.

scenes.title: Ancient Feuds
scenes.narration_text: Not disease. Not starvation. Other humans, smashing their heads with rocks over territorial disputes about berry bushes.
scenes.context: Describing the primitive and violent nature of ancestral conflicts.

scenes.title: From Rocks to ICBMs
scenes.narration_text: You've since upgraded the rocks to intercontinental ballistic missiles, but the berry bush energy remains.
scenes.context: Highlighting how technology has scaled but the underlying primitive aggression remains identical.

scenes.title: Selection of the Paranoid
scenes.narration_text: The tribes that survived weren't the peaceful, loving ones. They were the paranoid, survival-focused ones who:
scenes.context: Explaining natural selection's bias toward aggressive and wary groups.

scenes.title: Primal Defense
scenes.narration_text:
Assumed every stranger might want to kill them (often statistically accurate).

Struck first when threatened (natural selection at work).
scenes.context: Defining the behaviors that ensured survival in a hostile prehistoric environment.

scenes.title: Loyalty and Armament
scenes.narration_text:
Formed tight combat groups to kill other groups (teamwork!).

Hoarded weapons obsessively (can never have too many pointy sticks).
scenes.context: Describing group cooperation and the obsession with weapon accumulation as survival traits.

scenes.title: Modern Misplaced Preparation
scenes.narration_text:
Your brain is still running this exact software. That's why:

You spend more preparing to kill each other than preparing to not die.
scenes.context: Connecting ancient 'software' to current disproportionate spending on military vs healthcare.

scenes.title: Digital Combat
scenes.narration_text:
You instinctively distrust people who don't look like your tribe.

Twitter arguments feel like actual combat (your amygdala can't tell the difference).
scenes.context: How social media triggers the same biological responses as physical life-or-death fights.

scenes.title: Weapon Proliferation
scenes.narration_text:
Countries with thousands of nuclear weapons are worried they don't have enough.

The violence module kept your ancestors from getting clubbed to death.
scenes.context: Describing the logic of nuclear stockpiling as an extension of the primal violence module.

scenes.title: Biological Feature Creep
scenes.narration_text: Now it's building weapons that could end all life on Earth. Computer scientists call this "feature creep." Biologists call it "maladaptive."
scenes.context: Terminology for when a once-useful survival trait becomes destructive to the species.

scenes.title: Democracy's Hurdle
scenes.narration_text:
I call it "the reason I'm writing this book.".

The Tribal Brain (Or: Why Democracy Was Always Going to Be a Mess).
scenes.context: Moving from the Violence Module to the challenges of the 'Tribal Brain' in governance.

scenes.title: Dunbar's Number
scenes.narration_text: Dunbar's number says humans can maintain stable relationships with about one hundred and fifty people. That's your entire social capacity.
scenes.context: Defining the biological limit on the number of people a human can truly care about.

scenes.title: Filling the Slots
scenes.narration_text: Your brain has one hundred and fifty slots for caring about people, and you've filled most of them with coworkers you tolerate
scenes.context: How our limited social 'slots' are used up in modern society.

scenes.title: The Monkeysphere Boundary
scenes.narration_text:
and celebrities who don't know you exist.

Your brain treats anything outside your one hundred and fifty-person monkeysphere as an abstraction.
scenes.context: Describing the psychological wall between people we know and the rest of the world.

scenes.title: Dogs vs. Global Crises
scenes.narration_text:
That's why:

You care more about your neighbor's barking dog than ten thousand people dying of malaria (the dog is RIGHT THERE being loud,
scenes.context: An example of how proximity and tangibility override statistical importance in human empathy.

scenes.title: Tangible vs. Syllables
scenes.narration_text:
malaria is just a concept with numbers attached).

Local corruption makes you angrier than trillion-dollar Pentagon waste
scenes.context: Comparing our reaction to relatable local issues versus massive, abstract systemic problems.

scenes.title: The Pentagon's Trillions
scenes.narration_text: (the local guy stole ten thousand dollars you can imagine; according to Department of Defense, or D.O.D. audit failures,
scenes.context: Highlighting the difficulty humans have in conceptualizing massive sums of lost public money.

scenes.title: Face vs. Statistic
scenes.narration_text:
the Pentagon lost two point five trillion dollars, which is just syllables).

You'll donate to save one sick child but ignore statistics about millions
scenes.context: Explaining the identifiable victim effect—why one story moves us more than a dataset.

scenes.title: Civilization vs. Biology
scenes.narration_text:
(one child has a face, millions is just a very big number that makes your brain hurt).

Democracy asks this brain to make civilization-level decisions.
scenes.context: The conflict between our primal brains and the complex requirements of modern democracy.

scenes.title: Labradors and Taxes
scenes.narration_text: It goes exactly as well as asking a labrador retriever to do your taxes. You vote based on:
scenes.context: A humorous analogy for the incompetence of the human brain in modern political systems.

scenes.title: Visual Politics
scenes.narration_text:
Who looks stronger (your brain thinks the election is a wrestling match).

Who your tribe likes (if the clan approves, must be good).
scenes.context: Analyzing the primal shortcuts we use to choose political leaders.

scenes.title: Primordial Voting
scenes.narration_text:
Who makes you feel safe (fear sells better than policy ever will).

Who you'd have a beer with (relevance to nuclear policy: zero).
scenes.context: Concluding the list of irrational criteria used to judge modern candidates.

scenes.title: Primitive Leadership
scenes.narration_text: You elect leaders using the same brain circuits your ancestors used to pick the guy with the biggest club.
scenes.context: The narrator explains the evolutionary biological roots of modern political decision-making.

scenes.title: Evolutionary Preparation
scenes.narration_text:
Part 2: Genetic Slavery is Literally Killing Us.

Evolution prepared you for scarcity, predators, and violence.
scenes.context: Introducing the second part of the discussion, focusing on how evolution prepared humans for a different world.

scenes.title: Biological Mismatch
scenes.narration_text: You got abundance, safety, and Netflix. Your bodies responded with the biological equivalent of a computer trying to print a sandwich.
scenes.context: Describing the clash between ancient biological survival mechanisms and the modern world of abundance.

scenes.title: The Cosmic Joke
scenes.narration_text: Here's the cosmic joke: Humanity has never been safer, healthier, or more prosperous. You've also never been closer to wiping yourselves out.
scenes.context: Highlighting the irony of human history: being at our safest while being at our most vulnerable.

scenes.title: On-Brand Progress
scenes.narration_text:
You solved poverty and invented nuclear war in the same century. Very on-brand.

Problems you solved.
scenes.context: An observation on the contradictory nature of human achievement during the 20th century.

scenes.title: Food Waste
scenes.narration_text: Starvation (you throw away forty percent of food because storing it is inconvenient).
scenes.context: Explaining how starvation was solved, yet replaced with massive logistical waste.

scenes.title: Predator Extinction
scenes.narration_text: Predators (you murdered them into extinction, then put them in zoos so your children could see what you killed).
scenes.context: Describing the complete domination and subsequent display of former natural threats.

scenes.title: Infant Mortality
scenes.narration_text: Infant mortality (basically eradicated in developed countries, which makes the death rate in poor countries feel more optional and thus more tragic).
scenes.context: Reflecting on the eradication of childhood death in wealthy nations and the disparity elsewhere.

scenes.title: Infectious Diseases
scenes.narration_text: Most infectious diseases (vaccines work despite what Facebook says).
scenes.context: A commentary on modern medicine's success in controlling plagues and the social pushback.

scenes.title: Aging Miracle
scenes.narration_text: Dying at thirty (now you complain about turning forty, which your ancestors would consider a miracle worth celebrating daily).
scenes.context: Contrasting modern complaints about aging with the harsh life expectancy of our ancestors.

scenes.title: Nuclear Overkill
scenes.narration_text:
New problems you invented with your big brains:

Nuclear weapons (enough to end civilization thirteen times because once wasn't enough).
scenes.context: Transitioning into the new, self-inflicted existential threats created by advanced technology.

scenes.title: Accidental Terraforming
scenes.narration_text: Climate change (you're terraforming your only planet by accident).
scenes.context: Defining climate change as an unintentional and dangerous transformation of Earth's habitat.

scenes.title: Antibiotic Resistance
scenes.narration_text: Antibiotic resistance (ten million deaths annually by twenty fifty because you gave antibiotics to cows).
scenes.context: Explaining how livestock farming practices are creating a new global health crisis.

scenes.title: Sentient AI
scenes.narration_text: A.I. that might become sentient and decide you're the problem (the A.I. would be correct).
scenes.context: Sarcastic observation on the existential risk posed by artificial intelligence.

scenes.title: Social Media Torture
scenes.narration_text: Social media (voluntary psychological torture you pay for with attention).
scenes.context: Critiquing the modern digital environment as a form of self-inflicted mental strain.

scenes.title: Unqualified Triumph
scenes.narration_text: Eight billion gene copies and counting. From evolution's perspective, an unqualified triumph.
scenes.context: Evaluating human population growth from a purely biological and evolutionary success metric.

scenes.title: Disposable Meat Robot
scenes.narration_text: You're just the disposable meat robot they used to do it.
scenes.context: The narrator suggests that humans are merely vessels for genetic replication.

scenes.title: Toddler with Codes
scenes.narration_text: Humanity is a toddler who found the nuclear launch codes. Godlike technological power, hamster-level impulse control.
scenes.context: A metaphor for the dangerous gap between human technology and human emotional maturity.

scenes.title: The Five Percent
scenes.narration_text:
Part 3: Why You Can't Just "Be Better".

Your conscious mind controls maybe five percent of your decisions.
scenes.context: Beginning Part 3 by explaining the limits of human conscious willpower.

scenes.title: Ancient Software
scenes.narration_text: The other ninety-five percent is your ancient lizard brain running software older than agriculture. You think you're the pilot.
scenes.context: Explaining the dominance of subconscious, primitive brain functions in daily life.

scenes.title: Civilizational Passengers
scenes.narration_text:
You're actually a passenger who occasionally gets to suggest a direction.

This scales to civilization.
scenes.context: Applying the concept of lack of individual control to the macro-level of human society.

scenes.title: Amygdala Politics
scenes.narration_text: Your brain's fear center (amygdala) is directly connected to your voting finger. Politicians know this.
scenes.context: Explaining how political manipulation targets the biology of fear in the human brain.

scenes.title: Terror Override
scenes.narration_text: Say "terrorism" and your lizard brain overrides everything:
scenes.context: Describing how specific fear-inducing words trigger an immediate, irrational biological response.

scenes.title: Statistical Danger
scenes.narration_text:
More people die from falling out of bed than terrorism.

You're thirty-five thousand times more likely to die from heart disease.
scenes.context: Presenting actual statistical risks to highlight the irrationality of common human fears.

scenes.title: Faces vs Cholesterol
scenes.narration_text: But terrorism *feels* scarier, because evolution optimized your fear response for things with faces, not things with cholesterol.
scenes.context: Explaining why humans fear predators and violence more than lifestyle-related diseases.

scenes.title: Boring Slow Death
scenes.narration_text: The fear of violent death is older than language. The fear of slow death from disease? Your brain files that under "boring, deal with later."
scenes.context: Analyzing why the brain fails to prioritize protection against slow, chronic health threats.

scenes.title: Weapons vs Research
scenes.narration_text: Later never comes. Neither does the cure. That's why you spent two point seven two trillion dollars on weapons while cancer research got pocket change.
scenes.context: Critiquing global spending priorities based on primitive fear-based allocation of resources.

scenes.title: War on Furniture
scenes.narration_text:
Your bed is more dangerous than Al-Qaeda, but nobody's declared a War on Furniture.

Part Four: Breaking the Chains.
scenes.context: A humorous take on misplaced safety priorities, transitioning to the final section.

scenes.title: Universal Mortality
scenes.narration_text: Every single one of you is going to die. From the most powerful president to the lowliest pauper,
scenes.context: Stating the blunt reality of death that applies to all human beings regardless of status.

scenes.title: Escalating Suffering
scenes.narration_text: you face a life of gradually escalating suffering until it ends.
scenes.context: A sobering summary of the natural progression of life and aging.

scenes.title: Feeding Everyone
scenes.narration_text:
This is not a warning. It's a weather report.

You can feed everyone twice over, but you'd rather burn grain to keep prices high.
scenes.context: Calling out the systemic choice to maintain economic structures over humanitarian needs.

scenes.title: Selling Treatments
scenes.narration_text: You can cure diseases, but you'd rather sell treatments forever (cured customers don't come back; bad for quarterly earnings).
scenes.context: Critiquing the pharmaceutical industry for prioritizing recurring revenue over final cures.

scenes.title: Cave-dwelling Murderers
scenes.narration_text: You could be immortal space wizards. Instead you're cave-dwelling murderers with better tools.
scenes.context: Final closing statement on the gap between human potential and current behavior.

scenes.title: The Profit of War
scenes.narration_text: Because the current system makes irrationality profitable. Spectacularly profitable. Every bomb makes someone rich. Every missile funds a yacht.
scenes.context: The narrator explains how the current global system incentivizes war and destruction through high profits.

scenes.title: Profitable Diseases
scenes.narration_text: Every war creates a billionaire. Disease is profitable too. Not curing it, treating it. Insulin costs three hundred dollars a vial because dead
scenes.context: The narration shifts to the medical industry, illustrating how keeping people sick is more profitable than curing them.

scenes.title: The Chronic Illness Business
scenes.narration_text:
diabetics don't buy insulin. But cured diabetics don't either. So you keep them barely alive. It's good business.

The people making money from
scenes.context: Describing the economic logic behind treating symptoms rather than providing permanent cures for chronic conditions.

scenes.title: Rational Actors, Broken System
scenes.narration_text: war and disease aren't evil. They're just rational actors in a system that rewards the wrong things. You can't change human nature. Two hundred
scenes.context: The speaker argues that the problem isn't human evil, but a system that provides the wrong financial incentives.

scenes.title: Redesigning Profit Incentives
scenes.narration_text: thousand years of evolution doesn't care about your TED talk. But you can create economic systems that make curing people more profitable than
scenes.context: The narrative suggests that the only way to progress is to make humanitarian outcomes more profitable than destructive ones.

scenes.title: Evolutionary Mismatch
scenes.narration_text:
killing them. That's the only upgrade your species has ever responded to.

Expecting a brain built for hunting gazelles to handle nuclear policy,
scenes.context: Pointing out the massive gap between human biological evolution and the complex modern challenges we face.

scenes.title: The Calculator Analogy
scenes.narration_text: climate change, and a global economy is like expecting a calculator to run a space program. The calculator isn't broken. You're just asking it
scenes.context: Using a metaphor to explain that human brains are simply not designed for the scale of modern global problems.

scenes.title: Hacking Human Nature
scenes.narration_text:
to do something it was never built for. You can't fight two hundred thousand years of evolution.

But you can hack it. That's what a one
scenes.context: Transitioning from the problem of human limitations to a proposed solution: hacking our innate impulses.

scenes.title: Incentivizing Greed
scenes.narration_text:
percent treaty does. Instead of asking people to be rational (impossible), use their irrational impulses:

Greed: Make curing disease more
scenes.context: Explaining how a 'one percent treaty' leverages basic human greed to achieve better healthcare outcomes.

scenes.title: Political Fear and Tribalism
scenes.narration_text:
profitable than building bombs.

Fear: Make politicians more scared of voters than lobbyists.

Tribalism: Create an us-vs-disease tribe instead
scenes.context: Detailing how the treaty would redirect fear and tribalism toward beneficial goals like political reform and fighting disease.

scenes.title: Social Mechanics
scenes.narration_text:
of us-vs-them.

Social proof: Get three point five percent participation so others follow.

Immediate rewards: Pay people cash to join medical
scenes.context: Focusing on the psychological tactics of social proof and immediate cash rewards to drive global change.

scenes.title: The Genetic Prison
scenes.narration_text:
trials.

Your genes enslaved you in brains that fear strangers and cannot comprehend statistics. But they also gave you the ability to see the
scenes.context: Describing the biological constraints of the human mind and our unique ability to recognize them.

scenes.title: Uniquely Human Awareness
scenes.narration_text:
prison. No other animal can think: "Wow, my instincts are completely illogical." That's uniquely human. Use it.

A one percent treaty doesn't
scenes.context: Highlighting the meta-cognitive ability of humans to realize their instincts are flawed and using that realization as a tool.

scenes.title: Pragmatic Systems
scenes.narration_text: ask you to be better. It assumes you won't be, and redirects your worst impulses toward not dying. It's the only plan that works for the species
scenes.context: Asserting that the proposed treaty is realistic because it accepts human flaws rather than trying to fix them.

scenes.title: Designing for Reality
scenes.narration_text: you actually are, rather than the species you wish you were.
scenes.context: A final concluding thought on the importance of working with human nature as it truly exists.
